newsitem.title: JAPAN: MINOR METALS--COBALT SEEN LOOKING UP AFTER DLA BID.
newsitem.headline: MINOR METALS--COBALT SEEN LOOKING UP AFTER DLA BID.

text.p: Cobalt prices are set to resume their upward trend due to better-than-expected results for U.S. stockpile sales last week, traders said on Tuesday.
"The results (of U.S. stockpile sales) were higher than expected, which is underpinning the metal's price," said a trader. "The prices are looking upward."

Traders said the price of high-grade cobalt might climb towards $25 per pound in the near future, especially as production in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia remained low, while global demand was growing.
High-grade cobalt was quoted at $22.30/$23.20 per pound after a slight dip late last week, they said. Low-grade cobalt was quoted at $19.20/$20.00.

On Friday, the U.S. Defense National Stockpile Center said it sold 553,293 lbs of cobalt at an average price of $18.25 a lb, with the high bid by Powmet Inc at $18.8615 and the low bid by Glencore at $18.05.

Asked about a fire at a lithium-ion battery plant in Osaka on Sunday, one trader said although it might create additional demand for cobalt of about four tonnes, he was worried that the incident might harm the image of these type of batteries.
The Nikkan Kogyo Shimbun newspaper said on Tuesday the fire, caused by an explosion, destroyed about 400,000 lithium-ion batteries.

Traders said molybdenum oxide prices eased in quiet trade, while vanadium remained firm. Molybdenum oxide was quoted at $4.40/4.50 per pound. Vanadium pentoxide was sold at $4.17 per pound and ferro-vanadium was seen at around $20 per kilo.

A market source in Seoul said Posteel Inc, a Pohang Iron and Steel Co subsidiary, bought through tender 85 tonnes of ferro-vanadium from two South Korean companies last Friday at prices equivalent to $19.4-$19.6 per kg on CIF terms.
Arrival was set for October and November, the source said, adding the lowest bid from foreign firms was $19.85 CIF.
Little business was reported by minor metals traders in China.
One source in the southern province of Guangzhou reported hearing of a spot sale of bismuth at $3.00 per pound.
As the business was domestic, it would have no effect on C&F Rotterdam prices for the Chinese material, which remained unchanged from last week at $3.06/3.10 per pound, he said.
Antimony was plentiful although demand remained flat, traders said. Chinese material stored at ports on the southern tropical island of Hainan was available, but was going nowhere.

Prices remained soft, at around $1,900/1,950 per tonne, unchanged due to the lack of demand, one European source said. -- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai Newsroom +86-21-6279-8544 -- Yoo Chun Sik, Seoul Newsroom +82-2-727-5646 -- Nao Nakanishi, Tokyo Commodities Desk +81-3-3432-7431
